---
title: "stokesjx"
subtitle: "Instantaneous viscous response of a spherically symmetric mantle to internal loads (geoid, dynamic topography, surface velocity), in JAX, with derivatives"
---

## What this code does

`stokesjx` computes the instantaneous viscous (Stokes) response of a spherically
symmetric, self-gravitating mantle to internal density anomalies.

- **Kernels.** For each spherical-harmonic degree `l` and each source radius, the package
  computes four kernels. They are the geoid, the dynamic topography of the surface and of
  the core-mantle boundary (CMB), and the surface velocity.
- **Fields.** A field is the radial integral of a kernel times a density anomaly. The
  package also gives the free-air gravity anomaly and the admittance from the field
  coefficients.
- **Derivatives.** Every step is written in JAX. The kernels and the fields have
  derivatives with respect to the layer viscosities, the radii of movable viscosity
  boundaries and every other leaf of the radial profile. The derivatives are for
  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) over the radial viscosity
  ([derivatives](gradients.qmd)).

`stokesjx` is a propagator method in the variable `ln r`. For each degree, two sweeps of
a three-vector basis run through the mantle, one upward from the CMB and one downward
from the surface. After each interval the basis is orthonormalised. A single product of
the propagators of all intervals holds the growing and the decaying solutions together.
Their ratio over the mantle is about $(R/r_c)^{2l+3}$, which is 2e11 at `l = 20` and 1e27
at `l = 50`. The two sweeps keep each step well conditioned, so the method is stable in
float64 at every degree. [The physics page](physics.qmd) gives the equations and the
method, and [the validation page](validation.qmd) gives the benchmarks.

## Install

`stokesjx` needs Python 3.12 or later, NumPy, JAX and SciPy. Install the package from
PyPI:

```sh
pip install stokesjx
```

To change the code or to run the tests, clone the repository and install the package in
editable mode with the test dependencies:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/g-adopt/stokesjx
cd stokesjx
pip install -e ".[test,reference]"
```

The extras of `pyproject.toml`:

| Extra | Contents | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `test` | pytest, pytest-timeout, pytest-xdist, mpmath, sympy, PyYAML | the test suite |
| `reference` | `assess` | the tests against the analytical solutions of Kramer, Davies and Wilson (2021) |
| `docs` | quartodoc, griffe below 2 | the API reference of this site |

The package sets `jax_enable_x64` at import, so every array is float64. Each step of the
sweeps loses a few digits, and single precision leaves nothing for the derivatives.

## A forward run

A `RadialProfile` is the radial model: the node radii (CMB first), the reference density
`rho0` and the viscosity `eta` at the nodes, and the core. Two equal neighbouring radii
are a jump pair. A `StokesConfig` holds the static choices: the maximum degree, the
physics flags, the units and the numerical options. `stokes_kernels` is a pure function
of the two.

```python
import numpy as np
import stokesjx as sj

radius = np.linspace(3480e3, 6370e3, 65)                    # m, CMB first
rho0 = np.linspace(5500.0, 3300.0, 65)                      # kg/m^3
eta = np.where(radius > 5700e3, 1e21, 1e22)                 # Pa s
profile = sj.RadialProfile(radius, rho0, eta, core_density=9900.0)
config = sj.StokesConfig(lmax=20)

K = sj.stokes_kernels(profile, config)
assert K.degrees == tuple(range(1, 21))
assert K.geoid.shape == (20, 65)                            # (degrees, source nodes)
```

`Kernels` holds four arrays of shape `(L, N)`, one row per degree of `K.degrees` and one
column per source node, in SI units:

| Kernel | Unit | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `geoid` | m per kg/m² | geoid height at the surface |
| `surface_topography` | m per kg/m² | dynamic topography of the surface, outward positive |
| `cmb_topography` | m per kg/m² | dynamic topography of the CMB, outward positive |
| `surface_velocity` | m/s per kg/m² | coefficient of the root mean square horizontal speed |

A kernel is the response to a sheet of 1 kg/m² in one spherical harmonic at the source
node. `K.row(l)` gives the row of degree `l`. Where the frame rule refuses degree 1, the
rows start at `l = 2`.

A profile built from a new radius array compiles again. To change the viscosity or the
density, use `profile.replace(eta=...)`, which keeps the structure of the node table.

## Physics flags

`Formulation` holds five flags, and every one of the 32 combinations is solved:

| Flag | Values | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `gravity` | `GravityModel.FULL`, `GravityModel.NO_SELF_GRAVITY` | `FULL` |
| `background` | `Hydrostatic()`, `Uniform(value)` | `Hydrostatic()` |
| `compressible` | `False` (incompressible), `True` (TALA) | `False` |
| `surface` | `FreeSlip()`, `NoSlip()` | `FreeSlip()` |
| `cmb` | `FreeSlip()`, `NoSlip()` | `FreeSlip()` |

```python
form = sj.Formulation(gravity=sj.GravityModel.NO_SELF_GRAVITY, background=sj.Uniform(10.0),
                      compressible=True, surface=sj.NoSlip(), cmb=sj.FreeSlip())
K2 = sj.stokes_kernels(profile, sj.StokesConfig(lmax=20, formulation=form))
assert float(np.max(np.abs(np.asarray(K2.surface_velocity)))) == 0.0   # no slip at the surface
```

`DegreeOneFrame` is the frame request of degree 1. The default follows a static rule. It
gives the centre-of-mass frame for FULL with hydrostatic gravity and free slip at both
boundaries, and the raw frame for NO_SELF_GRAVITY or a uniform background. FULL with
hydrostatic gravity and a no-slip boundary has no degree 1 ([physics, section
10](physics.qmd#degree-1)).

## Fields

A density anomaly is an array with the radial axis first and the degree and order axes
last. For a real convention the `C/S` axis comes before them:
`(N, 2, Ld+1, Ld+1)`. `apply` integrates the four kernels against the density with the
trapezoid weights of the node table. A field has the layout and the convention of the
density.

```python
density = np.zeros((65, 2, 21, 21))                        # kg/m^3, real_4pi, CMB first
density[30:40, 0, 2, 0] = 10.0
F = sj.apply(K, density, profile)                           # F.geoid: (2, 21, 21), m

# The same field with explicit weights.
w = sj.quadrature_weights(profile)                          # (65,), m
F_w = sj.fields.radial_integral(K, density, w)
assert np.allclose(np.asarray(F_w.geoid), np.asarray(F.geoid), rtol=1e-15, atol=0.0)
```

`sh.CONVENTIONS` holds the three coefficient conventions:

| Convention | Shape | Normalisation |
|---|---|---|
| `complex_4pi` | `(..., L+1, L+1)` complex | 4π-normalised complex harmonics (lovejx) |
| `real_4pi` | `(..., 2, L+1, L+1)` real | 4π-normalised real harmonics (SHTOOLS, `.sph` density files) |
| `real_orthonormal` | `(..., 2, L+1, L+1)` real | orthonormal real harmonics (`SPHCO` coefficient files) |

`sh.convert` converts between them, and `sh.synthesis_grid` evaluates coefficients on a
latitude-longitude grid. The free-air gravity anomaly, the admittance and a weighted
spectral misfit are post-processing of the field coefficients:

```python
U = sj.sh.convert(F.geoid, "real_4pi", "complex_4pi")       # (21, 21) complex
lat = np.arange(89.0, -90.0, -2.0)                          # degrees north
lon = np.arange(-179.0, 180.0, 2.0)                         # degrees east
grid = sj.sh.synthesis_grid(F.geoid, "real_4pi", lat, lon)  # (90, 180), m

g_R = sj.surface_gravity(profile, config)                   # m/s^2
dg = sj.gravity_anomaly(F.geoid, g_R, radius[-1])           # m/s^2
Z = sj.admittance(dg, F.surface_topography, "real_4pi")     # (21,), s^-2
weights = np.where(np.arange(21) >= 2, 1.0, 0.0)
misfit = sj.spectral_misfit(F.geoid, np.zeros((2, 21, 21)), weights, "real_4pi")
assert np.all(np.isfinite(np.asarray(grid))) and np.isfinite(float(misfit))
```

## File formats

`stokesjx.io.legacy` reads and writes three text formats: the `.sph` density file
(`read_sph`), the viscosity file (`read_viscosity`) and the `SPHCO` coefficient files
(`read_sphco`, `write_sphco`). The package does not import the module, so import it on
use. Each data line of an `SPHCO` file holds `l`, `m`, `C` and `S` in this order.

```python
from stokesjx.io import legacy

coef = np.asarray(sj.sh.convert(F.geoid, "real_4pi", "real_orthonormal"))
legacy.write_sphco("SPH_geoid", coef, digits=16)            # es25.16e3, degrees 1 to 20
back = legacy.read_sphco("SPH_geoid")                       # (2, 21, 21), real_orthonormal
assert np.allclose(back[:, 1:], coef[:, 1:], rtol=1e-15, atol=1e-30)
```

## Examples

The directory `examples/` of the repository holds three scripts. Each script writes its
output to `--out` (default `examples/output/`).

| Script | Command | Output |
|---|---|---|
| forward run from a `.sph` density file | `python examples/forward_legacy_density.py --sph PATH --grid` | the four fields as `SPHCO` files, an npz file with the kernels and the fields, and with `--grid` the fields on a 1-degree grid |
| gradient of a geoid misfit against central differences | `python examples/gradient_layers.py` | a JSON summary |
| HMC over four layer viscosities and one movable boundary | `python examples/hmc_layers.py` | a JSON summary with the samples, the energy errors and the effective sample size |

`examples/earth_model.py` builds the PREM-like node table of the examples. The gradient
and the HMC example move one viscosity boundary with `Layers` by `motion="cut"`, the
default of `Layers` ([derivatives](gradients.qmd#movable-boundaries)).

## Run the tests

From an editable install, one command runs every test:

```sh
python -m pytest -n 8
```

The marker `slow` marks a test above about 30 s with `-n 8`. Use `-m "not slow"` for a
quick run. The tests that need local reference data or lovejx skip when the reference is
not installed.

## Build the documentation

```sh
make docs           # build the API reference and the site, then check both
make docs-preview   # render the site and serve it with live reload (no checks)
```

To build this site, install the extra `docs` and Quarto 1.10.18. `make docs` fails on a
parser message of the reference, a warning of the render, a parameter table that differs
from the signature, a broken link or display math that does not convert.

## Author

[Sia Ghelichkhan](https://sia-g.com) develops `stokesjx`. Parts of the package are ported
from lovejx (Sia Ghelichkhan, Jerry X. Mitrovica, William Scott and Mark Hoggard): the
layer parameterisation of the controls, the integration of gravity, the pattern of the
unit scales, the spherical-harmonic conventions and the Taylor-test policy. Agentic
coding tools wrote the implementation under the direction and review of the author
([agentic coding](agentic-coding.qmd)). [The citation page](citation.qmd) gives the
references for the software and the method.
